Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative primarily unfolds as a single, vivid scene in real-time, using concrete sensory details (the wet hemp, the rattling suitcase wheels, the cold steel lever), physical actions, and sparse dialogue to dramatize the emotional distance between Ilse and her son, Jonas. Rather than halting the narrative for lengthy blocks of exposition, the author weaves necessary background information seamlessly into the scene. Through brief moments of internal reflection and dialogue, the reader learns about Jonas's city life as a lawyer, the time passed since his last visit in autumn, the absence of Ilse's young helper, and Ilse's usual daily routine. This careful integration keeps the pacing tight and the reader fully engaged in the immediate tension of the moment while still providing all the context needed to understand their strained relationship.
